approaches.name: Deltopectoral
selection_indications: Common extensile exposure for primary reverse shoulder arthroplasty and the AO-recommended exposure for fracture reverse arthroplasty.
selection_limitations: Subscapularis management and repair depend on implant design, tissue quality, and surgeon plan.
positioning: Beach-chair positioning is commonly used; AO notes supine positioning may be used in selected conversion settings.
exposure: Develop the deltopectoral interval, protect the cephalic vein, mobilize the conjoint tendon judiciously, and manage the subscapularis/capsule according to the operative plan.

structures_at_risk.protection: Avoid prolonged or excessive medial retraction.

structures_at_risk.risk_phase: Inferior capsular release and humeral/glenoid exposure
structures_at_risk.protection: Maintain awareness of its inferior course and avoid blind inferior dissection.

pitfalls: Inadequate protection of the axillary nerve during inferior release
questions: Q: What is the superficial interval? A: The deltopectoral interval, with deliberate management of the cephalic vein.
Q: Which nerve is threatened by aggressive conjoint tendon retraction? A: The musculocutaneous nerve.
approaches.coverage_notes: Fracture reverse arthroplasty adds tuberosity-specific exposure and repair priorities.

approaches.name: Anterolateral / superolateral deltoid split
selection_indications: Alternative exposure used by some surgeons and implant workflows.
selection_limitations: Axillary nerve and deltoid injury are defining concerns; AO does not recommend it for fracture reverse arthroplasty.
positioning: Positioning and incision vary with the selected anterolateral or superolateral technique.
exposure: Split the deltoid in line with its fibers only within a defined safe extent and maintain direct awareness of the axillary nerve.

structures_at_risk.risk_phase: Distal extension of the deltoid split
structures_at_risk.protection: Limit and control the split; identify or palpate the nerve when the exposure requires it.
Preserve deltoid origin and continuity because reverse arthroplasty depends on deltoid function.

pitfalls: Extending the split into the axillary nerve
questions: Q: Why is deltoid preservation particularly important in reverse arthroplasty? A: Reverse mechanics rely on a functioning deltoid for elevation.
Q: What is the defining neurologic risk of a deltoid split? A: Axillary nerve injury from distal extension or retraction.
approaches.coverage_notes: Alternative approach; the case context must distinguish elective primary RSA from fracture RSA.
